hidden.g: Located or positioned out of sight; not visually apparent.

hide.e: From Middle English hiden, huden, from Old English hȳdan (“to hide, conceal, preserve”), from Proto-West Germanic *huʀdijan (“to conceal”), from Proto-Germanic *huzdijaną (“to hoard”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewdʰ- (“to cover, wrap, encase”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- (“to cover”).
hide.g: To put (something) in a place where it will be out of sight or harder to discover.

hide.e: From Middle English hyde, from Old English hȳd, from Proto-West Germanic *hūdi, from Proto-Germanic *hūdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *kéw(H)tis (“skin, hide”) (compare Latin cutis (“skin, rind, hide”)), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kew(H)- (“to cover”), ultimately the same root as the above etymology.

high.e: From Middle English high, heigh, heih, from Old English hēah (“high, tall, lofty, high-class, exalted, sublime, illustrious, important, proud, haughty, deep, right”), from Proto-West Germanic *hauh (“high”), from Proto-Germanic *hauhaz (“high”), from Proto-Indo-European *kewk- (“to bend; crooked”).
high.g: Physically elevated, extending above a base or average level:

high.e: From Middle English hegen, heghen, heien, a conflation of Old English ġehēgan (“to perform, conduct”) (from Proto-West Germanic *hauwjan) and hēan (“to raise up, exalt”) (from *hauhijan), also influenced by heigh (“high”).

highly.e: From Middle English hiȝly, heȝly, heyȝliche, from Old English hēalīce (“highly”), equivalent to high + -ly.
highly.g: In a high or esteemed manner.

highness.e: From Middle English hyghnesse; equivalent to high + -ness.

highway.e: From Middle English heiȝwai, heiȝwei, from Old English hēahweġ (“main road, highway”), corresponding to high + way.
highway.g: A main public road, especially a multi-lane, high-speed thoroughfare.

hill.e: From Middle English hil (“hill”), from Old English hyll (“hill”), from Proto-West Germanic *hulli (“hill”), from Proto-Germanic *hulliz (“hill”), from Proto-Indo-European *kl̥Hnís (“top, hill, rock”) (compare also Proto-Germanic *halluz (“stone, rock”)).
hill.g: An elevated landmass smaller than a mountain.

hilltop.g: The peak or crest of a hill.

himself.e: From Middle English hymself, from Old English him selfum. Equivalent to him + -self.
himself.g: Him; the male object of a verb or preposition that also appears as the subject

hin.e: From Middle English hin, from Latin hin, from Hebrew הִין, from Egyptian h:n-nw-w-W22 (hnw, “jar, unit of liquid volume”).
hin.g: A former Hebrew liquid measure of volume (about 3.8 L).

hind.e: From Middle English hinde, from Old English hindan (“at the rear, from behind”), Proto-Germanic *hinder (“behind, beyond”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱem-ta- (“down, below, with, far, along, against”), from *ḱóm (“beside, near, by, with”).
hind.g: Located at the rear (most often said of animals' body parts).

hind.e: From Middle English hynd, hine, from Old English hī(ġ)na, genitive plural of hīġa (“servant, family member”), in the phrase hīna fæder ‘paterfamilias’. The -d is a later addition (compare sound).
hind.g: A servant, especially an agricultural labourer.

hinder.e: From Middle English hinder, comparative form of hind: more hind.
hinder.g: Of or belonging to that part or end which is in the rear or hind, or which follows.

hindermost.e: From Middle English hintirmest, hyndermest, hyndermeste, hyndirmaste; equivalent to hinder + -most.

hindquarter.g: Either rear half of a side of beef, mutton, veal, lamb or by extension from another edible mammal.

hindrance.e: From Middle English hinderance, hinderaunce, hindraunce, hynderaunce, hynderawnce, hynderawns, hyndrance; equivalent to hinder + -ance.
hindrance.g: Something which hinders: something that holds back or causes problems with something else.

hinge.e: From Middle English henge (“hinge”), from Old English *henġ or *henġe (“hinge”), from Proto-West Germanic *hangiju or *hangī; compare Old English *henġe- in henġeclif (“overhanging cliff”), Old English henġen (“hanging; that upon which a thing is hung”).
hinge.g: A jointed or flexible device that allows the pivoting of a door etc.

hint.e: From Middle English hinten, hynten, variant of henten (“to lay hold of, catch”), from Old English hentan (“to seize, grasp”), from Proto-West Germanic *hantijan, from Proto-Germanic *hantijaną. Related also to hunt.

hip.e: From Middle English hipe, hupe, from Old English hype, from Proto-Germanic *hupiz (compare Dutch heup, Low German Huop, German Hüfte), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewb- (compare Welsh cysgu (“to sleep”), Latin cubāre (“to lie”), Ancient Greek κύβος (kúbos, “hollow in the hips”), Albanian sup (“shoulder”), Sanskrit शुप्ति (śúpti, “shoulder”)).
hip.g: The outward-projecting parts of the pelvis and top of the femur and the overlying tissue.

hip.e: From Middle English hepe, heppe, hipe, from Old English hēope, from Proto-Germanic *heupǭ (compare Dutch joop, German Hiefe, Faroese hjúpa), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewb- (“briar, thorn”) (compare Old Prussian kaāubri (“thorn”), Lithuanian kaubrė̃ (“heap”)).

hire.e: From Middle English hire, hyre, here, hure, from Old English hȳr (“employment for wages; pay for service; interest on money lent”), from Proto-West Germanic *hūʀiju (“payment”), from the verb *hūʀijan, from Proto-Germanic *hūzijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *kewHs- or *kweHs-.
hire.g: A person who has been hired, especially in a cohort.

hire.e: From Middle English hiren, hyren, from Old English hȳrian (“to hire”), from the noun (see above). Eclipsed Middle English souden (“to hire, employ, enlist”), borrowed from Old French souder, soudre, souldre (“to take into employ, pay”); see obsolete English sold (“salary, military pay”).
hire.g: To obtain the services of in return for fixed payment.

hireling.e: From Middle English hirlyng, from Old English hȳrling (“hireling, employee”), from Proto-West Germanic *hūʀijuling. By surface analysis, hire + -ling.
hireling.g: An employee who is hired, often to perform unpleasant tasks with little independence.

hiss.e: From Middle English hissen, probably of onomatopoeic origin (compare Arabic هَسْهَسَ (hashasa)).
hiss.g: A sibilant sound, such as that made by a snake or escaping steam; an unvoiced fricative.

hit.e: From Middle English hitten (“to hit, strike, make contact with”), from Old English hittan (“to meet with, come upon, fall in with”), from Old Norse hitta (“to strike, meet”), from Proto-Germanic *hittijaną (“to come upon, find”), from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂eyd- (“to fall; fall upon; hit; cut; hew”).
From Middle English hit (“it”), from Old English hit (“it”), from Proto-Germanic *hit (“this, this one”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱe-, *ḱey- (“this, here”).

hitch.e: Probably from Middle English hicchen, hytchen, icchen (“to move; to move as with a jerk”), of obscure origin. Lacks cognates in other languages.

hither.e: From Old English hider, from Proto-Germanic *hidrê.

hitherto.e: The adverb is derived from Middle English hiderto (“to the present time, until now; up to this point”), from hider (“in this direction, to or toward this place; up to the present time, until now”) (from Old English hider (“to here, hither”)) + to (“in the direction of, toward; etc.”). By surface analysis, hither + to.
hitherto.g: Up to this or that time.
